articleHeader.subtitle: A complete beginner-friendly guide to Python iterators — iterable vs iterator, iter(), next(), StopIteration, building custom iterator classes, and the itertools module.

sections.title: What is an Iterator in Python?

blocks.text: An iterator in Python is an object that represents a stream of data — it produces one value at a time, on demand, and remembers exactly where it left off between calls. Every for loop you have ever written in Python — over a list, string, dictionary, or file — is secretly powered by an iterator behind the scenes.

Formally, Python defines an iterator as any object that implements two special methods: __iter__(), which returns the iterator itself, and __next__(), which returns the next value in the sequence — or raises a StopIteration exception when there are no more values left. This pair of methods together is called the iterator protocol.

Iterators are one of Python's most elegant and quietly powerful features. They allow you to process sequences of unknown or even infinite length without loading the entire sequence into memory at once — a capability that becomes essential when working with huge files, network streams, or generated data.

sections.title: Iterable vs Iterator — The Most Important Distinction

blocks.text: Beginners frequently confuse an iterable with an iterator — the two terms sound similar but describe fundamentally different things. Understanding this distinction is the single most important concept in this entire topic.

An iterable is any object you can loop over — a list, tuple, string, set, or dictionary. Technically, it's any object that implements __iter__(), which returns a fresh iterator. An iterator is the object actually doing the work of producing values one at a time — it implements both __iter__() and __next__(), and it keeps track of its current position, which an iterable itself does not do.

This is the key takeaway: a list is iterable (it knows how to produce an iterator), but a list is not itself an iterator (it has no __next__() method and no memory of position). Once you call iter(numbers), you get an actual iterator that does have both methods.

sections.title: The iter() and next() Built-in Functions

blocks.text: Python provides two built-in functions that form the practical entry point to the entire iterator system: iter() converts an iterable into an iterator, and next() retrieves the following value from that iterator.

Once every value has been produced, calling next() one more time raises a StopIteration exception — this signals to whatever is consuming the iterator (like a for loop) that there is nothing left to retrieve. Crucially, once exhausted, an iterator cannot be reset or reused — you must call iter() again on the original iterable to start over.
next() also accepts an optional default value, letting you avoid the StopIteration exception entirely — similar in spirit to how dict.get() avoids a KeyError.

blocks.text: Every for loop in Python is simply syntactic sugar around the iterator protocol. When you write for item in my_list:, Python performs a precise, repeatable sequence of steps automatically, entirely hidden from view.

sections.title: Building Your Own Custom Iterator Class

blocks.text: Any Python class can become an iterator by implementing both __iter__() and __next__(). This is a foundational technique for building custom, memory-efficient sequences — for example, a counter that counts up to a limit.

Walking through this class: __init__() sets up the starting state — a limit and a current counter starting at 0. __iter__() simply returns self, since the object itself already knows how to produce values. __next__() is where the real logic lives: it checks whether the limit has been reached, and either raises StopIteration or increments and returns the next number.
Because CountUpTo implements the full iterator protocol, it works seamlessly not just in for loops, but with any built-in function that expects an iterable — list(), sum(), max(), and more.

sections.title: Why Custom Iterators Are Often Single-Use

blocks.text: A subtle limitation of the CountUpTo class above is that once exhausted, it cannot be reused — its __iter__() returns self, which is the same object with current already at its limit.

The second call returns an empty list because the same exhausted iterator object was reused. This is exactly how many of Python's own built-in iterators behave too — a file object, once fully read, produces no more lines even if you try to iterate it again without reopening it.

To make a class truly reusable across multiple loops, separate the roles: make the class an iterable (with __iter__() that returns a brand-new iterator object each time) rather than an iterator itself.

Now every call to iter(numbers) creates a fresh CountUpTo object with its own independent state, so the same CountUpToIterable object can be looped over as many times as needed — this is precisely how built-in lists and tuples behave.

sections.title: Generators — A Simpler Way to Build Iterators

blocks.text: Writing a full class with __iter__() and __next__() works, but Python offers a dramatically simpler shortcut for building iterators: generator functions, which use the yield keyword instead of return.

This single function replaces the entire CountUpTo class from earlier. Every time yield executes, the function's state is paused, its value is handed to whoever called next(), and execution resumes exactly where it left off on the following call. Python automatically implements __iter__() and __next__() for you behind the scenes — this deep topic deserves its own dedicated guide, linked below.

sections.title: The itertools Module — Iterator Building Blocks

blocks.text: Python's standard library ships with itertools, a module packed with fast, memory-efficient functions for creating and combining iterators — covering infinite sequences, combinatorics, and grouping operations, all without ever loading a full sequence into memory.

items.html: itertools.count(start, step) — Produces an infinite sequence of evenly spaced numbers, starting from start.
itertools.cycle(iterable) — Repeats the given iterable's elements infinitely, looping back to the start once exhausted.
itertools.repeat(value, times) — Repeats a single value a specified number of times, or forever if times is omitted.
itertools.chain(iter1, iter2) — Combines multiple iterables into a single continuous iterator, without creating an intermediate combined list.
itertools.islice(iterable, stop) — Slices an iterator lazily, useful for taking a limited number of values from an otherwise infinite iterator.
itertools.permutations(iterable) — Generates all possible orderings of the given iterable's elements.
itertools.combinations(iterable, r) — Generates all possible r-length combinations of elements, without regard to order.

blocks.text: Note the use of islice() to safely take only the first five values from itertools.count(1) — since count() produces values infinitely, calling list() directly on it would run forever and never return.

sections.title: How Iterators Work Internally — Memory Efficiency

blocks.text: The core motivation behind the iterator protocol is lazy evaluation — producing values one at a time, only when requested, rather than computing and storing an entire sequence upfront. This is what allows Python to represent sequences that would be impossible to hold in memory all at once, such as reading a 50 GB log file line by line.

When you open a file in Python, the file object itself is an iterator — calling next() on it (or looping over it with for line in file:) reads and returns exactly one line at a time from disk, never loading the entire file's contents into memory simultaneously. This is a direct, practical benefit of the iterator protocol that would be impossible if Python only supported fully materialized lists.

This same lazy-evaluation principle is why itertools.count() can represent an infinite sequence without crashing your program — no memory is allocated for values that haven't been requested yet, and the sequence simply continues producing values on demand, forever, until you explicitly stop consuming it.
Try modifying the code below to experiment with manual iteration. Add another next() call after the loop ends and observe the StopIteration exception.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Using Iterators

pros.title: Memory Efficient
pros.text: Iterators produce one value at a time rather than holding an entire sequence in memory, making them ideal for very large or infinite data sources.

pros.title: Uniform Interface
pros.text: Any object implementing __iter__ and __next__ works seamlessly with for loops and built-in functions like list(), sum(), and max().

pros.title: Supports Infinite Sequences
pros.text: Since values are computed lazily, iterators can represent sequences with no defined end, such as itertools.count().

pros.title: Enables Lazy Evaluation
pros.text: Computation only happens when a value is actually requested, avoiding wasted work on values that are never used.

pros.title: Foundation for Generators
pros.text: Understanding the iterator protocol makes generators — Python's simpler, more common tool for lazy sequences — far easier to understand.

cons.title: Single-Pass by Default
cons.text: Most iterators are exhausted after one full traversal and cannot be reset without recreating them from the original iterable.

cons.title: No Direct Indexing
cons.text: Unlike a list, you cannot access the 'third value' of an iterator directly — values are only available in sequence, one at a time.

cons.title: More Verbose for Simple Cases
cons.text: Writing a full class-based iterator requires more boilerplate code than achieving the same result with a generator function.

cons.title: Harder to Debug
cons.text: Since values don't exist until requested, inspecting an iterator's full contents mid-debugging (without consuming it) requires extra care, such as using itertools.tee().

sections.title: Real-World Use Cases of Python Iterators

items.strong: 📄 Reading Large Files Line by Line
items.text: — Processing multi-gigabyte log files or CSV files uses the file object's built-in iterator to read one line at a time, keeping memory usage constant regardless of file size.
— Custom iterator classes are commonly built to fetch and yield pages of results from a web API one at a time, hiding the pagination logic behind a simple for loop.
— Data processing pipelines chain multiple iterators together, transforming and filtering records one at a time as they flow through, without ever materializing the full dataset in memory.
— Systems that need to generate unique sequential IDs commonly use itertools.count() as an infinite, thread-safe-friendly counter.
— Mathematical sequences like Fibonacci numbers or prime numbers are frequently implemented as custom iterators or generators, since their length is unbounded.
— Database libraries return query results as an iterator over rows, fetching each row from the database only as it's requested rather than loading the entire result set upfront.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between an iterable and an iterator?
items.a: An iterable is any object that can be looped over and implements __iter__(), such as a list or string — it returns a new iterator each time __iter__() is called. An iterator is the object that actually produces values one at a time via __next__(), and it remembers its current position, unlike the iterable itself.

items.q: Q2. What two methods must a class implement to be a valid iterator?
items.a: __iter__(), which must return the iterator object itself (usually self), and __next__(), which returns the next value in the sequence or raises StopIteration when there are no more values left. This pair of methods is collectively known as the iterator protocol.

items.q: Q3. What happens when an iterator is exhausted, and can it be reused?
items.a: Once exhausted, calling next() again continues to raise StopIteration — the iterator does not reset itself. To iterate over the same data again, you must create a fresh iterator using iter() on the original iterable, since a used-up iterator object holds no more values to give.

items.q: Q4. What does a for loop actually do internally with an iterable?
items.a: A for loop calls iter() once on the iterable to obtain an iterator, then repeatedly calls next() on that iterator, executing the loop body with each returned value, until a StopIteration exception is raised, which the loop catches internally and uses as a signal to exit cleanly.

items.q: Q5. What is the difference between a class-based iterator and a generator function?
items.a: A class-based iterator requires manually implementing __iter__() and __next__(), managing state through instance attributes. A generator function uses the yield keyword inside a regular function, and Python automatically handles state-pausing and the iterator protocol implementation, making generators far more concise for most use cases.

items.q: Q6. Why can itertools.count() be used without running out of memory, despite being infinite?
items.a: Because it uses lazy evaluation — each value is computed only when requested via next(), and no values are pre-computed or stored in memory ahead of time. This is fundamentally different from generating a list of infinite numbers, which would be impossible.

items.q: Q7. What is the purpose of the StopIteration exception?
items.a: StopIteration signals that an iterator has no more values to produce. It is raised inside __next__() when the sequence is exhausted, and Python's for loop automatically catches this exception internally, using it purely as a termination signal rather than letting it propagate as an error to your code.

items.q: Q8. Is a Python string an iterable, an iterator, or both?
items.a: A string is an iterable, not an iterator — it implements __iter__() (which returns a new string iterator each time) but not __next__() directly. Calling iter('abc') produces a genuine iterator object that does implement __next__(), following the same pattern as lists and tuples.

items.q: Q9. How would you make a custom iterator class reusable across multiple for loops?
items.a: Separate the roles into two classes: an iterable class whose __iter__() method returns a brand-new instance of a separate iterator class each time it's called, rather than returning self. This ensures every fresh loop starts with a clean, independent iterator state.

items.q: Q10. What is the difference between next(iterator) and next(iterator, default)?
items.a: next(iterator) raises a StopIteration exception if the iterator is exhausted. next(iterator, default) instead returns the specified default value silently in that case, avoiding the exception entirely — useful for safely peeking at the next value without crashing the program.

items.q: 1. What is the output of: it = iter([1, 2]); print(next(it)); print(next(it)); print(next(it))?
items.a: 1, 2, then a StopIteration exception is raised on the third call, since the iterator has only two values and has now been fully exhausted.

items.q: 2. Is calling iter() on a list that is already an iterator necessary, or is a list itself already an iterator?
items.a: A list is only an iterable, not an iterator — it does not implement __next__(). Calling iter(my_list) is necessary to obtain an actual iterator object before next() can be used on it.

items.q: 3. Write a custom iterator class that produces only even numbers up to a given limit.
items.a: class Evens: def __init__(self, limit): self.limit = limit; self.current = 0. def __iter__(self): return self. def __next__(self): self.current += 2; if self.current > self.limit: raise StopIteration; return self.current

items.q: 4. Why does looping over the same exhausted iterator object twice in a row produce no output the second time?
items.a: Because an iterator has no way to reset its internal position once __next__() has raised StopIteration — its state permanently reflects being fully consumed. A new iterator must be created from the original iterable to loop over the same data again.

items.q: 5. What is the output of: print(list(itertools.islice(itertools.count(5, 2), 4)))?
items.a: [5, 7, 9, 11]. itertools.count(5, 2) produces an infinite sequence starting at 5, incrementing by 2 each time, and islice() safely limits it to the first 4 values before it would run forever.

items.q: 6. Explain why file objects in Python are considered iterators.
items.a: A file object implements both __iter__() (returning itself) and __next__() (which reads and returns the next line from disk). This allows for line in open('file.txt') to work directly, reading one line at a time lazily rather than loading the entire file into memory.

items.q: 7. How would you convert a generator function into an equivalent class-based iterator?
items.a: Move the generator's local variables into instance attributes set in __init__(), implement __iter__() to return self, and translate the function's logic and yield points into conditional return statements inside __next__(), raising StopIteration explicitly where the generator would have simply ended.

items.q: 8. What is the difference between itertools.chain() and simply concatenating two lists with +?
items.a: itertools.chain(list_a, list_b) lazily combines both iterables into a single iterator without creating a new combined list in memory — values are produced on demand as you iterate. list_a + list_b immediately creates a brand-new, fully materialized list containing all elements from both, using more memory upfront.

sections.title: Conclusion — Why Iterators Matter in Python

blocks.text: Iterators are the quiet engine powering nearly every loop you write in Python — from a simple for loop over a list, to reading a massive log file line by line, to processing an infinite stream of sensor data. Understanding the iterator protocol — __iter__() and __next__() — demystifies what Python is actually doing every time you iterate over anything.

The single most important distinction to internalize: an iterable is something you can loop over (like a list), while an iterator is the object actually doing the looping, one step at a time, remembering exactly where it is. Every iterable knows how to produce a fresh iterator; an iterator itself is typically single-use and gets exhausted after one full pass.

items.q: What is the difference between iter() and next() in Python?
items.a: iter() converts an iterable (like a list) into an iterator object, which is the object capable of producing values one at a time. next() is then called on that iterator to actually retrieve each subsequent value, raising StopIteration once all values have been produced.

items.q: Is every iterable also an iterator in Python?
items.a: No. An iterable, like a list or string, only needs to implement __iter__(), which returns a new iterator when called. It does not itself implement __next__() or track position, so a list on its own is not an iterator — you must call iter() on it first to get one.

items.q: What is the iterator protocol in Python?
items.a: The iterator protocol refers to the two special methods, __iter__() and __next__(), that any object must implement to behave as an iterator. __iter__() returns the iterator itself, and __next__() returns the next value or raises StopIteration when exhausted — this is what for loops rely on internally.

items.q: Can a Python iterator be reused after it's exhausted?
items.a: No, not directly. Once an iterator raises StopIteration, it remains exhausted — calling next() again will keep raising the same exception. To iterate over the same data again, you must call iter() on the original iterable to obtain a completely new iterator object.

items.q: What is the difference between a generator and an iterator?
items.a: Every generator is an iterator, but not every iterator is a generator. A generator is created using a function with yield (or a generator expression), and Python automatically handles the underlying __iter__() and __next__() implementation. A class-based iterator requires you to write those methods manually yourself.
